scoring_rationale.architecture: reports.py is now a 20-line hub composing focused mixins, and Engram cleanly composes Retrieval/Context/Reconcile/Reports in core.py:64. The remaining architectural drag is mcp_server.py at 1411 lines plus telemetry side effects inside wrappers.
scoring_rationale.testing: 490 tests pass, total coverage is 83%, and mcp_server.py is 86%. tests/test_mcp_coverage.py has many real persistence/error assertions, but telemetry integration and full 43-tool tracking are not directly protected.
scoring_rationale.security: Telemetry is opt-in/local-only in telemetry.py:174 and setup_wizard.py:685, XSS escaping is centralized in reports_review.py:28, and path hygiene rejects NUL bytes. Main gap: payload validation ignores dict keys.
scoring_rationale.documentation: README stats match actual test/coverage/tool counts, and SECURITY.md now explains opt-in usage stats. However CONTRIBUTING.md still says no telemetry, docs/comparison.md keeps v3.14.2 numbers, and architecture line counts drift.
scoring_rationale.positioning: The identity-layer positioning remains clear and differentiated: cross-tool, local-first, user-owned JSON, MCP-native. Trust wording around usage statistics is now mostly repaired, but residual old docs weaken the promise.

top_3_issues.title: Telemetry payload validator ignores dictionary keys
top_3_issues.detail: _validate_payload walks payload values but never validates keys. Because tool call names are encoded as dict keys, a future caller could accidentally log natural-language content or paths as a key even though long/natural-language values are rejected. Current mcp_server uses fixed literal names, so this is not an active leak in normal use, but the safety boundary is weaker than the docs imply.

top_3_issues.title: Usage statistics do not cover the full MCP tool surface
top_3_issues.detail: mcp_server.py exposes 43 tools, but _track is only called for the Tier-1-style subset. Tools such as ingest_notes, extract_session_insights, update_knowledge, archive_knowledge, review_knowledge, start_project, import/export helpers, and resources are not counted. Also wrap_up_session flushes before recording its own call, so the session-ending tool is excluded from that day's flush.

top_3_issues.title: Documentation still has stale privacy and baseline claims
top_3_issues.detail: README and SECURITY are mostly aligned, but CONTRIBUTING.md still says '100% local - no cloud, no telemetry, no external calls'. docs/comparison.md still reports 386 tests / 78% coverage from v3.14.2, and docs/telemetry_roadmap.md labels Phase 2 as v3.16.0 even though v3.16.0 currently ships Phase 1 local-only behavior.

top_3_strengths.title: Facts match the headline release quality claims
top_3_strengths.detail: The required commands verified 490 passed tests, 83% total coverage, 86% mcp_server.py coverage, and 43 @mcp.tool wrappers.

top_3_strengths.title: Reports split is clean and low-risk
top_3_strengths.detail: reports.py is a thin composition hub, with rarity/review/identity/analytics separated into understandable mixins and the public ReportsMixin import preserved.

top_3_strengths.title: Privacy UX is substantially better than typical telemetry
top_3_strengths.detail: Usage statistics are default-off, setup explains exact fields, preview/status/off commands exist, Phase 1 has no network, and SECURITY.md documents the boundary.

next_3_priorities.title: Harden telemetry before any network phase
next_3_priorities.why: Validate dict keys, restrict tool names to a fixed allowlist, add mcp_server integration tests for all tracked tools, and record wrap_up_session before flushing.

next_3_priorities.title: Finish documentation consistency sweep
next_3_priorities.why: The project sells trust. Any stale 'no telemetry' or old test-count claim will look worse than the actual code.

next_3_priorities.title: Plan the next mcp_server.py decomposition
next_3_priorities.why: reports.py was successfully split, but mcp_server.py is now the largest file at 1411 lines and carries transport, auth, resources, wrappers, tiering, and telemetry integration.

comparison_with_deepseek.agree_or_disagree: Overall I agree with DeepSeek's 7.53 direction and land at 7.6. I score testing higher because I ran the complete suite and saw real wrapper/persistence/error assertions, not just superficial calls. I score security lower because full-source review found the telemetry validator key blind spot and incomplete tool tracking. Documentation is slightly higher than DeepSeek because README/SECURITY are now substantially repaired, but still capped by stale CONTRIBUTING/comparison/roadmap claims.
